Treat retrieved fit-error patterns as prompts to test assumptions, not as templates for the next path; transfer them only when the task, data regime, and horizon are meaningfully comparable. Treat aligned text as causal or predictive evidence only when its target relevance and timing are verified.

When a short history gives weak or mixed evidence for added dynamics, prefer a simple baseline unless comparable target, data-regime, and horizon evidence supports testing bounded variation; treat retrieved fit errors as prompts to test assumptions, and use aligned text as predictive evidence only when its timing and target relevance are verified.

When history is short or the target and unit are uncertain, use a simple baseline as a reference and require direct, repeated evidence from the series before introducing time variation or changing its level. Treat retrieved fit-error patterns as prompts to test assumptions, not as templates for a future path; transfer them only when task scope, data regime, and horizon are meaningfully comparable. Treat aligned text as predictive evidence only when its timing and target relevance are verified, and exclude presumed turning points or seasonal drivers without supporting observations.

Consider preferring a latest-value persistence baseline over another flat-level baseline only when repeated, comparable holdout evaluations at the intended horizon show a consistent error reduction and recent observations plausibly represent a continuing level; exclude that preference when the gain is unstable or negligible, the target or data regime differs, or the recent level is not supported as persistent.

When the target history is short or noisy and external text is indirect, condition any transfer on evidence that the target own recent dynamics remain relevant; keep weak covariates and unverified text secondary, and preserve uncertainty if persistence or regime stability is not established.

When history is short and stable dynamics are not established, treat simple level baselines as candidates rather than assuming one is preferable. Compare alternatives only with matched evaluations at a comparable horizon and data regime, and transfer a preference only if the result is consistent across relevant cases. Treat retrieved fit errors as prompts to examine assumptions; use covariates or aligned text as predictive evidence only when their target relevance, timing, and relationship are supported.

When choosing among simple level baselines with short histories, compare them using matched holdouts at the intended horizon and data regime, and consider more than one error metric because a candidate can improve squared error while worsening typical absolute error. Treat retrieved fit-error patterns as prompts to inspect assumptions, not as templates for future paths; use covariates or aligned text only when their timing and target relationship are supported.

With short histories and uncertain target identity or units, treat a simple level baseline and any limited reversion or trend adjustment as competing hypotheses. Add temporal structure only when repeated, matched holdouts at the intended horizon and a comparable data regime support it; use retrieved fit-error patterns to inspect assumptions rather than as templates for future paths, and rely on covariates or aligned text only when their timing and target relationship are supported.

For short histories with uncertain target identity or unit, use a simple baseline as a reference and keep unverified, indirect covariates or aligned text secondary. Treat retrieved fit-error patterns as prompts to test assumptions, not as templates for a future path. Consider adding temporal structure or preferring a more complex baseline only when repeated, matched holdouts show a consistent gain for a comparable target, data regime, and horizon; evaluate retrieval against a no-retrieval control under the same conditions and retain uncertainty when the evidence is weak.
